title: Real-Time FPGA-Based Multi-Parameter Feedback Stabilization of a Silicon Double Quantum Dot
authors: Johnathan Bryan, Tim J. Wilson, Hong-Wen Jiang
abstract: Long term operation of semiconductor spin qubits requires active stabilization of quantum dot potentials against low-frequency charge noise. Previous work demonstrated a gradient-descent feedback (GDFB) approach on a silicon double quantum dot utilizing transport current measurements. We extend such a GDFB approach in a silicon double quantum dot device with high-bandwidth rf-reflectometry readout by utilizing a field-programmable gate array, the OPX by Quantum Machines, for digital signal processing. The OPX enables continuous multi-parameter gradient calculation and quick gate voltage updates, significantly increasing the effective feedback bandwidth compared to previous work. By operating with 8 steps per feedback cycle and an integration time of 25.6 $μ$s, this high speed stabilization scheme achieves a -6 dB noise suppression up to a bandwidth of 5 kHz. This effectively suppresses low frequency 1/f noise, maintaining device stability over longer time periods, and potentially enables real-time control in large-scale quantum dot arrays.
summary: The paper reports an advanced experimental technique to stabilize silicon double quantum dots against disruptive low-frequency charge noise using a fast, multi-parameter feedback loop implemented via FPGA and RF-reflectometry. This method significantly increases the effective feedback bandwidth to 5 kHz, which is crucial for maintaining qubit coherence in solid-state quantum computing architectures.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is actively stabilizing quantum dot potentials against low-frequency 1/f charge noise to enable long-term operation of semiconductor spin qubits.
main_result: The high-speed feedback scheme successfully suppressed low-frequency 1/f noise, achieving a -6 dB noise suppression up to a bandwidth of 5 kHz.
method: The authors extended the Gradient-Descent Feedback (GDFB) approach by integrating high-bandwidth RF-reflectometry readout with an FPGA controller for continuous multi-parameter gradient calculation and fast gate voltage updates.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a Silicon Double Quantum Dot (DQD) fabricated on a heterostructure, which serves as the physical platform for semiconductor spin qubits.
key_observables: Low-frequency 1/f charge noise, and the in-phase component of the reflected microwave signal used to measure potential shifts.
important_parameters: The achieved noise suppression bandwidth is 5 kHz, significantly surpassing previous limits based on DC transport measurements. The feedback cycle time dictates a theoretical maximum cutoff frequency of $\sim 6.1 \text{ kHz}$.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation noted is that the current feedback bandwidth is constrained by the total feedback cycle time ($\approx 81.8 \mu\text{s}$ per cycle).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, show Power Spectral Density (PSD) comparisons demonstrating noise suppression with and without feedback, and plot the measured attenuation of the PSD as a function of perturbation frequency.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of active stabilization for spin qubits, introduces the advanced GDFB protocol using RF-reflectometry on an FPGA platform, presents results showing high-bandwidth noise suppression, and concludes by discussing future work related to coherence time characterization.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing: decoherence due to environmental charge noise. The implementation of real-time, high-bandwidth feedback control is highly relevant for building scalable quantum processors.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the experimental setup. The double quantum dot, located at the 60 mK stage, is coupled to an RF-reflectometry circuit for fast dispersive readout. The reflected signal is amplified and demodulated, while a Quantum Machines OPX provides digital signal processing and voltage control

FIG. 2. (a) Power spectral density of the in-phase signal component showing the 1/ f noise present in our system. Data was taken at the point corresponding to 0 output voltage as shown in (b). This spectrum is generated by overlaying traces from multiple runs, shown by the different point colors. (b) Device charge stability diagram. Feedback was initialized at a minimum in the interdot transition signal, occurring at approximately zero output voltage.

FIG. 4. Power spectral density of the in-phase component with a 300 Hz sinusoidal perturbation applied to the device. The solid red line represents the spectrum with the feedback loop disabled, while the dashed black line is with feedback enabled.
FIG. 5. Measured attenuation of the in-phase signal power spectral density as a function of the applied perturbation frequency.

FIG. 3. Time-domain response of the feedback protocol. (a) shows the in-phase signal over time as recorded by the OPX. The sinusoidal perturbation is clearly shown. (b) shows the output voltages applied by the OPX to the device.
